notes:
Need to search first.I've written notes for all 25 verses. Most come from older commentaries, and the Protestant differences are clearest on baptism (v. 1) and election (v. 12). My research tools hit their usage limit partway through, so some things you asked for are missing:

- **Pages I couldn't fully read.** I read Enduring Word (Guzik) only up to v. 18; the rest of the page didn't load. For Pulpit, Gill, Ellicott, Precept Austin and the Biblehub verse pages I only had search-result extracts, not whole pages. A missing comment doesn't mean the commentator says nothing.
- **Sites I didn't reach at all.** I got nothing from netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org, newadvent.org, catholic.com or oca.org. So there are no modern-scholarship, Catholic or Orthodox readings below, and nothing on prosperity or hyper-grace teaching. I also found nothing Pentecostal or Methodist-specific.
- **Names.** Biblehub's verse pages mix several old commentaries, and the extracts often didn't say which one was speaking. Where that happened I say "a note on the page" rather than guess a name.

---

**v. 1**
- Guzik: Paul now turns to practical living, but it rests on doctrine. We can only seek things above because we really were raised with Christ, an idea Paul pictured with baptism in 2:12. Guzik suggests that, like the risen Jesus, believers leave the tomb, serve others, live by the Spirit's power and look toward heaven. With N.T. Wright, he reads "right hand of God" (Psalm 110) as Christ's present rule. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/colossians-3/
- Ellicott: Sharing Christ's death taught the negative lesson (death to the Law). Sharing His resurrection teaches the positive one, the spiritual life. Compare Philippians 3:20 on heavenly citizenship. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/colossians/3.htm
- Pulpit Commentary: Paul moves from argument to practice without breaking his thought. Believers overcome the flesh by rising above it, not by fighting it with rituals and strict self-denial. "Things above" are not abstract ideas; they are "where Christ is." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/colossians/3.htm
- Precept Austin: The theme is "be what you are": live out in practice the position you have in Christ. The "if" states something certain. https://www.preceptaustin.org/colossians-3-commentary
- Gill: Paul assumes they really are risen with Christ. They rose as members of Christ their head when He rose, and "emblematically" in their baptism. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/colossians/3.htm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/colossians/3-1.htm
- **Traditions differ: what baptism does.**
  - Lutheran (1517.org): "Raised with Christ" points back to 2:12 and is rooted in baptism, echoing Romans 6. The new life hidden in Christ starts at your baptism as God's own work with ongoing effects, and the writer links this to Luther's emphasis. https://www.1517.org/articles/epistle-colossian-31-4-easter-sunday-series-a-2026 ; https://www.1517.org/articles/epistle-colossians-31-11-pentecost-8-series-c-2025
  - Baptist (John Piper, Desiring God, on 2:11–12, which 3:1 builds on): Going under and coming out of the water is not what unites you to Christ; faith does. We are justified at our first act of faith, and baptism follows as a sign. https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/is-baptism-necessary-for-salvation
  - GotQuestions also speaks of being raised with Christ "through believer's baptism," meaning we are identified with His death, burial and resurrection. https://www.gotquestions.org/raised-with-Christ.html
  - On the Biblehub verse page, one older preacher says "sacramentarian" readers claim the Colossians rose with Christ *in* baptism; he rejects that and calls baptism the "speaking sign." Another note says the language fits adult baptism better than infant baptism. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/colossians/3-1.htm
- **Traditions differ: Christ "seated" above.** An older note on the same page argues that Christ's local ascension and session make the Lutheran argument for His body being present everywhere unsound. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/colossians/3-1.htm

**v. 2**
- Guzik: The best Christian living comes from minds fixed on heaven. He quotes Vaughan: earthly things aren't all evil, but even harmless ones do harm if they take heaven's place. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/colossians-3/
- Gill: Food, clothing and daily needs may be provided for, but not anxiously, and happiness must not be placed in them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/colossians/3-2.htm
- Notes on the same page:
  - Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: whatever we make an idol becomes a cross to believers or a curse to unbelievers.
  - The Geneva Study Bible reads "earth" as the show of religion criticised in chapter 2.
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/colossians/3-2.htm

**v. 3**
- Ellicott: Better "ye died." It means both death to sin and death to the visible world. The spiritual life is hidden, has its source in God, and is kept up by communion with Him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/colossians/3.htm
- Gill: Believers are dead to the law, to sin's condemning power, and to the world. Their life is safe in God, so they can never perish. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/colossians/3.htm
- Precept Austin:
  - John Eadie quotes Luther: we live not in the flesh but dwell in it.
  - A.B. Simpson: this life is hidden from the world, from the devil who cannot steal it, and sometimes from our own feelings.
  https://www.preceptaustin.org/colossians_33-5
- ICC: "Died" points to a single past moment, while "is hidden" describes the state that now results. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/icc/colossians/3.htm

**v. 4**
- Ellicott: This is the last stage, when Christ's appearing reveals what is now hidden and completes what exists only as a seed. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/colossians/3.htm
- Guzik: We won't only see Christ's glory; we will share it. He quotes Wright: Paul and the humble Colossians will then be seen as they truly are. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/colossians-3/
- Pulpit: Believers will be revealed with Him, including the redemption of the body (Romans 8:19, 23). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/colossians/3-4.htm
- A note on the same page: Christ is literally the essence of the Christian's life, not merely the one who gives it. Another note says a perfect church shouldn't be expected before then, and criticises Rome for trying to set up a church that already reigns in triumph. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/colossians/3-4.htm

**v. 5**
- Guzik:
  - "Put to death" is very strong (Vaughan): wipe out the old life, don't just control it.
  - Naming sins matters (Wright).
  - He quotes G. Campbell Morgan on why greed is idolatry and so destructive.
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/colossians-3/
- Ellicott: The "members" to kill are the old man's vices that live in them. "Inordinate affection" means passion. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/colossians/3.htm
- Gill: The greedy person treats money like an idol, trusting and almost worshipping it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/colossians/3.htm
- Notes on the verse page: Paul means sin living in the members, not the body itself. One note says the tense describes decisive action repeated at each temptation, and that "sinless perfection" can't be drawn from this verse because Paul treats his converts as still imperfect. It names no group. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/colossians/3-5.htm

**v. 6**
- Gill: God's wrath means judgment now and eternal ruin, and only Christ delivers from it. "Sons of disobedience" are those who reject both law and gospel. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/colossians/3.htm
- Guzik: Partly, wrath comes as God lets people go on in self-destructive sin (Romans 1). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/colossians-3/
- Lange's commentary records that Ellicott takes the wrath as punishment both now and hereafter. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lange/colossians/3.htm

**v. 7**
- Ellicott: They were "living in" paganism, with evil spreading on every side. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/colossians/3.htm
- Guzik: These sins are past tense for Christians. They may sometimes happen, but they must not be a believer's walk. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/colossians-3/

**v. 8**
- Guzik: These "little" sins of speech are no more acceptable than the sexual sins; bridle the tongue. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/colossians-3/
- Ellicott: "Filthy language" here means coarse insult and abuse more than impurity. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/colossians/3.htm
- Gill: Mainly obscene talk, though it covers all corrupt speech. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/colossians/3.htm

**v. 9**
- Guzik quotes Barclay: you can lie without words, by a tone, a look or a silence. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/colossians-3/
- Gill: Lying is worse among believers because they are members of one body. Some ancient versions read "you have taken off" as a command. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/colossians/3.htm
- ICC: Most commentators take "since you have taken off" as the reason for the commands. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/icc/colossians/3.htm

**v. 10**
- Guzik: Clothing language. The image is now that of the second Adam, Christ. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/colossians-3/
- Precept Austin:
  - Putting on the new man happened at salvation (our standing before God), yet we must "wear" daily what God made.
  - W.E. Vine: this is the new creation at the new birth.
  - It rejects a teaching that believers become "little gods," without naming who teaches it.
  https://www.preceptaustin.org/colossians_310
- Gill: The Spirit renews the new nature day by day. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/colossians/3.htm

**v. 11**
- Guzik: The new family breaks down racial, class and cultural barriers. He gives Bruce's examples of slave and free martyrs, Blandina, and Perpetua with Felicitas. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/colossians-3/
- Pulpit: Christ is our common centre and the life of His people, and all human distinctions must bow to Him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/colossians/3.htm
- Notes on the verse page: the Scythian is the extreme case of a barbarian (Bengel: "more barbarous than barbarians"). This principle also settles small church quarrels. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/colossians/3-11.htm
- Gill tells the story of Anacharsis the Scythian. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/colossians/3.htm

**v. 12**
- Guzik: "Elect" should comfort us and give us a calling to fulfil. Every virtue listed is about relationships (Barclay). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/colossians-3/
- **Different emphases on election** (none labels them by tradition):
  - Gill: chosen in Christ from eternity by God's sovereign will.
  - Another note: "elect" means all true disciples who believe so as to be pardoned and renewed.
  - Pulpit: "holy and beloved" follow from election rather than decide it.
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/colossians/3-12.htm

**v. 13**
- Guzik: Christ's forgiveness is the pattern and makes us more generous. He quotes Spurgeon: "I forgive but can't forget" is a lame forgiveness. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/colossians-3/
- Precept Austin: Literally "forgiving yourselves," so the whole church forgives one another, with no limit. https://www.preceptaustin.org/colossians_312-25
- Ellicott: The manuscripts favour "Lord," but it makes no real difference. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/colossians/3-13.htm

**v. 14**
- Ellicott: Love is the belt holding all the other virtues together. False teachers claimed perfection through knowledge for a few; Paul places it in love, open to everyone. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/colossians/3.htm
- Guzik: Love is the outer garment. Without it the other virtues get distorted (Wright). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/colossians-3/

**v. 15**
- Guzik: "Rule" means "act as umpire" (F.B. Meyer, Adam Clarke): choose what makes for peace. Wright says this is peace in the community, not only inside one person. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/colossians-3/
- Pulpit: Christ's peace secures believers against false teachers. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/colossians/3.htm

**v. 16**
- Ellicott: "In all wisdom" goes with the teaching, matching "in grace singing." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/colossians/3.htm
- Guzik: The three song types point to variety more than strict categories. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/colossians-3/
- **Worship music** (I couldn't confirm any Reformed source on psalm-only singing):
  - A writer quoted by Precept Austin notes that English-speaking churches once sang only metrical psalms for centuries.
  - Another, from *Today in the Word*, calls church music wars a violation of this verse.
  https://www.preceptaustin.org/colossians_3-16_commentary
  - Piper (Baptist) suggests "spiritual songs" may include songs the Spirit gives in the moment. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-mighty-ministry-of-song

**v. 17**
- Guzik: All of life should be lived for Jesus, doing only what can be done in His name. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/colossians-3/
- Precept Austin uses the picture of power of attorney: acting in someone's name. https://www.preceptaustin.org/colossians_317-25
- Pulpit: Thanksgiving goes along with daily talk and work. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/colossians/3.htm

**v. 18**
- Guzik: "Submit" is a military word, "to be under in rank." Submitting is to a role, not because one person is worth less. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/colossians-3/
- Pulpit: In each pair the junior party is addressed first. Ephesians 5 gives the spiritual reason. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/colossians/3.htm
- Sam Storms: Submission is voluntary yielding to a recognised authority and is first of all obedience to Christ. It never means following a husband into sin, and it isn't oppressive. https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/wives-who-submit-to-their-husbands--3:18-
- Bible.org: Submission holds for every age and culture because it is "fitting in the Lord." https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-24-submissive-wives-really-colossians-318
- Bible.org (another series): "In the Lord" means fitting for Christians. https://bible.org/seriespage/8-husbands-and-wives-analogues-christ-and-church-ephesians-521-and-colossians-318-19
- Matthew Henry: Submission is to her own husband, not to a tyrant. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/colossians/3.htm
- Every source I found here holds the husband-headship (complementarian) view. I found no egalitarian reading.

**v. 19**
- Ellicott: "Do not grow bitter"; don't let yourself become exasperated. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/colossians/3.htm
- Pulpit: Bitterness means exasperation that leads to hasty harshness; Bengel calls it "hatred mixed with love." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/colossians/3.htm
- Precept Austin: William Kelly says husbands can let life's pressures crowd out care for their wives. The verse gives no comfort to the chauvinist. https://www.preceptaustin.org/colossians_317-25

**v. 20**
- Matthew Henry: Dutiful children are the most likely to prosper. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/colossians/3.htm

**v. 21**
- Ellicott: The better text reads "do not provoke" (as in "stir up"), meaning constant restless prodding, "spurring the willing horse," which ends in discouragement. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/colossians/3.htm
- Pulpit: Endless demands and complaints teach a child to see the father as an enemy. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/colossians/3.htm
- Precept Austin: Fathers should treat children as God treats His. https://www.preceptaustin.org/colossians_320-25

**v. 22**
- Ellicott: The emphasis on slaves probably reflects the presence of Onesimus, the runaway slave. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/colossians/3.htm
- Matthew Henry: Obey in everything that fits duty to God; God-fearing servants are faithful even when unwatched. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/colossians/3.htm
- Biblehub study note: Slavery was part of Roman life; earthly masters' authority is only temporary. https://biblehub.com/study/colossians/3-22.htm
- Precept Austin (Eadie): the real Master is Christ. https://www.preceptaustin.org/colossians_320-25

**v. 23**
- Pulpit: Even humble tasks are honoured by being done for the Lord. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/colossians/3.htm
- Gill: In context this verse is aimed at servants. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/colossians/3.htm
- Matthew Poole: work cheerfully even under harsh masters. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/colossians/3-23.htm
- Precept Austin: The workshop and the barn become temples. https://www.preceptaustin.org/colossians_320-25

**v. 24**
- Ellicott: No slave could inherit; only a son could. So the slave on earth is recognised as a son in heaven. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/colossians/3.htm

**v. 25**
- Matthew Henry: The righteous Judge deals justly between master and servant; both stand equal before Him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/colossians/3.htm
